title: Kathina
hook: at the end of the rains lay people offer cloth for new robes

segments.voice: Yesterday, a day of mindfulness at home, and your line: a retreat at home. Is your quiet half-day on the calendar yet? Day one hundred fifty-five.
screen: `A DAY AT HOME — A RETREAT AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Thirty monks set out to see the Buddha. They're forest monks from a town called Pava, and they've planned to spend the rainy season near him at Savatthi. But the start of the rains catches them on the road, six yojanas short, as the text counts it. The rule is the rule: stay in one place. So they spend three whole months stuck in a town called Saketa, close enough to picture him, too far to reach. When the retreat ends, they set off, through rain and deep mud, and arrive soaked, their robes filthy and heavy with water. What happens next, tradition says, is the root of a festival Theravada monasteries still keep after the rains. Today: Kathina.
screen: `THIRTY MONKS ON THE ROAD.` → `THE RAINS CATCH THEM.` → `THEY ARRIVE SOAKED.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Vinaya, the monastic rulebook. The Buddha welcomes the thirty travelers, asks how their retreat went, and hears about the waiting and the mud. And he responds with a new allowance: at the end of the rains, monks who have kept the retreat may receive cloth and make new robes. That is the kathina. The word means firm, or hard, and tradition explains it as the wooden frame the cloth was stretched on for sewing. In the old practice, the whole community worked together, cutting, sewing and dyeing, to finish a robe in a single day. Here's the part that makes it a festival. Monks aren't allowed to ask for cloth. It has to be offered. So lay people do the offering. Within a month after the rains end, in Thailand, Laos, Myanmar, Sri Lanka and Cambodia, families and whole villages organize kathina ceremonies. There are processions, music, food, money trees hung with small gifts for the monastery, and at the center, a bolt of cloth. And notice who receives it. The cloth is given to the community as a whole, not to one favorite monk. The monks then agree together which of them will receive it, traditionally one whose robes are most worn. The rains began with staying still; they end with giving. Three months of monks practicing in one place, then a day when the people around them say thank you with something useful. Not money for its own sake, not a trophy: cloth, for the robe a monk wears every day.
screen: `A NEW ALLOWANCE: CLOTH FOR ROBES.` · `KATHINA — THE FIRM FRAME.` · `MONKS CAN'T ASK; IT MUST BE OFFERED.` · `GIVEN TO THE WHOLE COMMUNITY.` · then, large: `THE RAINS END IN GIFTS.`

segments.voice: Sit easily and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone who has been steady for you lately: a colleague, a neighbor, a teacher, someone at home. Think about what they actually use. Not a trophy, something useful. A meal, a tool, a warm pair of socks, an hour of help, a book they mentioned. Let one gift come to mind. Notice the gladness of planning it, the first of the three gladnesses you met in the giving week. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Kathina. The robe-cloth offering at the end of the rains, named for the firm frame the cloth was stretched on.
Your line: the rains end in gifts. Today, give something useful to someone who has been steady for you. Keep it simple and practical. Day one hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: In Theravada countries, within a month after the rains retreat ends, lay people hold kathina ceremonies with processions and food, offering robe cloth and other necessities to the monastic community.

fork.setup: you're one of the thirty monks. the rains begin while you're still six yojanas from the Buddha. what do you do?
options: keep walking; seeing him matters more.
stop and keep the retreat where you are.
fork.reveal: they kept the rule and spent the rains at Saketa, then went to him soaked the moment it ended. the Buddha answered with the kathina.

original.note: Pali: firm or hard; likely the frame used to stretch cloth for sewing robes.

trapdoor: what you thought: kathina is a Buddhist harvest festival.
what it means: the offering of robe cloth to the monastic community at the end of the rains retreat.
what a scholar hears: Mahavagga VII opens with the thirty Paveyyaka monks; kathina, 'firm,' is usually explained as the frame on which robe cloth was stretched.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga VII.1 (Kathina Khandhaka), the thirty monks of Pava

notes: Editor review (days 151-169): Mahavagga VII.1 does not say the rains came early; now 'the start of the rains catches them', six yojanas as the text counts; 'across Asia' narrowed to Theravada; kathina etymology attributed to tradition.

Story details paraphrased from Mahavagga VII.1: thirty forest monks from Pava, rains begin at Saketa (six yojanas from Savatthi, given here as 'about a week's walk'), arrive soaked; confirm the distance phrasing.
Etymology of kathina as the frame for stretching cloth is the common explanation; scholars discuss alternatives. Flagged as 'thought to'.
Robe 'finished in a single day' reflects the traditional rule that the kathina robe be completed on the day of offering; confirm.
Link back to the 'glad three times' teaching (day 133) in the practice.
Kathina is a Theravada observance; Mahayana communities differ.
